panpsychism-vs-idealism.title: Panpsychism vs Idealism
panpsychism-vs-idealism.seoTitle: Panpsychism vs Idealism: Goff, Kastrup and the Debate
panpsychism-vs-idealism.metaDescription: Panpsychism gives matter an inner life. Idealism makes matter a form of mind. Compare the two views, the Goff–Kastrup debate and the problems each faces.
intro: Panpsychism and idealism both reject the materialist claim that consciousness arises from wholly nonconscious matter. They disagree about what to put in its place. Panpsychists such as Philip Goff, Galen Strawson and David Chalmers keep the physical world and give it an inner nature. Following Bertrand Russell, they note that physics describes what particles and fields do and says nothing about what they are in themselves. That intrinsic nature, they propose, is experience or something close to it.

Idealists go further. In Bernardo Kastrup’s analytic idealism there is one universal consciousness, and the physical world is how its activity looks from outside. Individual minds are dissociated parts of it, much as alters form in dissociative identity disorder. Matter is real as appearance, with nothing beneath it that is not mind.

Goff and Kastrup have debated the question in public several times, and their exchanges show where the views split. Kastrup presses the combination problem. If every particle has its own tiny experience, nobody has explained how billions of them add up to one unified human subject. Goff replies that idealism faces the same puzzle run backwards, the decomposition problem of how one cosmic mind splits into many private ones, and that it must also explain why mind behaves with the lawful regularity physics describes. Each side holds that its own problem is the easier one to solve.

The choice reaches beyond metaphysics. The two views give different answers on whether machines could be conscious and whether anything of a person survives death, and the stances below show where individual theories land.
panpsychism-vs-idealism.commonGround: Both treat consciousness as fundamental, and both cite the hard problem as their main reason for rejecting materialism. Both accept the findings of physics and neuroscience and reinterpret what those findings describe. Each faces a mirror-image unity problem, combining small minds into one or dividing one mind into many.

differences.a: Physical entities whose intrinsic nature is experiential or proto-experiential. Matter is real and has an inner side.
differences.b: Consciousness alone. The physical world is how mental activity appears from outside, or exists only within mind.

differences.a: Simple micro-experiences combine into human and animal minds, by a process no one has yet explained.
differences.b: One universal consciousness divides into many. Kastrup calls individual minds dissociated alters of it.

differences.a: Keeps physics as it is and supplies the intrinsic nature its structural descriptions leave out, following Russell.
differences.b: Treats physics as a description of regularities within experience, with nothing outside mind for it to describe.

differences.a: The combination problem. Nobody has shown how tiny subjects add up to one unified mind.
differences.b: The decomposition problem. Idealists must explain how one mind splits into many and why the shared world is so lawful.

differences.a: Open. AI hardware has the same basic ingredients as a brain, and whether they form a subject depends on the combination problem.
differences.b: Kastrup calls conscious AI a fantasy, since computation alone does not make a dissociated center of experience.

iit-vs-global-workspace-theory.title: Integrated Information Theory vs Global Workspace Theory
iit-vs-global-workspace-theory.seoTitle: IIT vs Global Workspace Theory: Key Differences
iit-vs-global-workspace-theory.metaDescription: Integrated Information Theory and Global Workspace Theory are two of the most tested theories of consciousness. Compare claims, evidence and AI verdicts.
intro: Integrated Information Theory (IIT) and Global Workspace Theory (GWT) are two of the most discussed scientific accounts of consciousness, and they start from opposite ends. Giulio Tononi built IIT from experience itself. He lists features every experience has, such as being unified and specific, and asks what kind of physical system could have them. His answer is a system with high integrated information, measured as Φ (phi), whose parts constrain each other in ways that cannot be split.

Bernard Baars proposed GWT in the 1980s, working from cognitive psychology. The brain runs many specialized processes in parallel, and information becomes conscious when it enters a limited-capacity workspace and is broadcast to all of them. Stanislas Dehaene and Jean-Pierre Changeux developed this into the Global Neuronal Workspace, in which conscious access appears as a sudden, brain-wide ‘ignition’ across prefrontal and parietal cortex.

For GWT, consciousness is what a brain does with information, so any system with the right architecture could have it. For IIT, consciousness is what a physical system intrinsically is, its cause-effect structure, so a conventional computer running brain-like software would have almost none. The theories also point to different brain regions, IIT to a posterior ‘hot zone’ and GWT to frontal and parietal networks.

Those clear differences made them natural targets for an adversarial collaboration. In the Cogitate Consortium, proponents of both theories agreed on predictions before the data came in. The results, published in Nature in 2025, contradicted key predictions of each theory and settled neither. After early results were presented in 2023, an open letter signed by more than a hundred researchers called IIT pseudoscience, a charge David Chalmers and others rejected.
iit-vs-global-workspace-theory.commonGround: Both are scientific theories that try to say which physical systems are conscious and make predictions brain data can test. Both accept that most brain activity is unconscious and treat conscious experience as unified. Their proponents agreed to test them head to head under predictions fixed in advance.

differences.a: Integrated information. An experience is identical to a system’s maximally irreducible cause-effect structure.
differences.b: Global availability. Content becomes conscious when it is broadcast across the brain to many specialized processes.

differences.a: Phenomenology. Axioms about experience are translated into postulates about physical systems.
differences.b: Cognitive psychology and neuroscience, especially lab contrasts between conscious and unconscious processing.

differences.a: Mainly posterior cortex, where IIT expects sustained, highly integrated activity.
differences.b: A frontal and parietal network that ‘ignites’ when a stimulus reaches awareness.

differences.a: Counterintuitive predictions, such as consciousness in simple but highly integrated grids, and a Φ measure impractical to compute for real brains.
differences.b: It explains access and reportability, and critics say it leaves open why broadcast information feels like anything.

differences.a: Conventional digital computers have negligible Φ, so they would not be conscious however intelligent they seem.
differences.b: Possible in principle. A machine with a global workspace architecture could meet the theory’s conditions.

materialism-vs-idealism.title: Materialism vs Idealism
materialism-vs-idealism.seoTitle: Materialism vs Idealism: Does Mind or Matter Come First?
materialism-vs-idealism.metaDescription: Materialism says consciousness comes from matter. Idealism says matter comes from consciousness. Compare how each explains the mind, the brain and the world.
intro: Materialism and idealism are mirror images. Materialists hold that the world is physical through and through and that consciousness is something brains do. It is the working assumption of most neuroscientists, and it rests on the close dependence of experience on the brain. Damage the visual cortex and sight goes; anesthetize the brain and experience stops. Materialist theories range from U. T. Place and J. J. C. Smart’s identity theory to Global Workspace Theory and Daniel Dennett’s illusionism.

Idealists reverse the order. Mind is basic, and the physical world exists within consciousness or as its appearance. George Berkeley argued that to be is to be perceived. Advaita Vedānta identifies the self with Brahman, ultimate reality. Today Bernardo Kastrup treats individual minds as dissociated parts of one universal consciousness, and Donald Hoffman argues that the world is made of interacting conscious agents.

Each side’s strength is the other’s problem. Materialism fits the success of physical science but faces what David Chalmers named the hard problem. Even a complete account of neural activity seems to leave open why that activity feels like anything. Idealism avoids that problem, since experience is its starting point, but owes an account of why a world made of mind follows stable laws that hold for everyone, and why private minds depend so closely on brains. Kastrup’s answer is that a brain is what a dissociated mind looks like from outside.
The two also part ways on death. Materialists expect consciousness to end with the brain, while idealists such as Kastrup expect individual experience to rejoin a wider consciousness.
materialism-vs-idealism.commonGround: Both are monist views. Each says reality is made of one kind of thing and rejects the dualist split between mind and matter. Both accept the same experimental findings about brains and experience, and they disagree about what those findings ultimately describe.

differences.a: Physical particles, fields and the laws that govern them.
differences.b: Consciousness. Matter is a form mind takes, or a pattern within it.

differences.a: The brain produces or constitutes consciousness, which is why brain changes alter experience.
differences.b: The brain is the outward image of mental activity, so the two track each other without the brain creating mind.

differences.a: The hard problem. Physical descriptions seem to leave out why experience feels like anything.
differences.b: Explaining a lawful, shared world, and how one mind divides into many private ones.

differences.a: Third-person science. Consciousness is studied through brain imaging, lesions and behavior.
differences.b: Philosophical argument from the primacy of experience, with appeals to parsimony and to evidence such as psychedelic brain imaging.

differences.a: Experience ends when the brain stops working.
differences.b: Varies by theory. Kastrup expects personal experience to merge back into universal consciousness at death.

differences.a: Possible on functionalist and computational versions, doubted on biological ones such as John Searle’s.
differences.b: Kastrup calls conscious AI a fantasy. Other idealists leave the question open.

dualism-vs-materialism.title: Dualism vs Materialism
dualism-vs-materialism.seoTitle: Dualism vs Materialism: Is the Mind More Than the Brain?
dualism-vs-materialism.metaDescription: Dualism says the mind is more than the brain. Materialism says it is entirely physical. Compare their arguments, objections and answers on life after death.
intro: Dualism and materialism give opposite answers to the oldest question about the mind. Dualists hold that consciousness involves something nonphysical. In René Descartes’s substance dualism, the mind is a thinking thing distinct from the extended body. Property dualists, including David Chalmers in his naturalistic dualism, keep one physical substance but give it irreducible mental properties. Dualism is also the default teaching of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

Materialists hold that consciousness is entirely physical, a product of brains and bodies with nothing left over. It is the working assumption of most neuroscientists, and in the 2020 PhilPapers survey just over half of professional philosophers accepted or leaned toward physicalism.

The arguments run in both directions. Dualists point to the explanatory gap. In Frank Jackson’s thought experiment, Mary knows every physical fact about color but has never seen red, and she seems to learn something new when she first does. Chalmers argues that a physical duplicate of you with no experience, a ‘zombie’, is conceivable. Materialists answer with the interaction problem, first pressed on Descartes by Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia. If physics is causally closed, it is hard to see how a nonphysical mind could move a neuron. They add that brain damage and drugs change experience in precise ways, and that Occam’s razor counts against a second kind of thing.
Much rides on the outcome. Substance dualism leaves room for a soul to survive death, while materialism ties the mind’s fate to the brain’s.
dualism-vs-materialism.commonGround: Both accept that in ordinary life experience depends closely on the brain. Interactionist dualists such as Karl Popper and the Nobel-winning neuroscientist John Eccles used the same brain science materialists rely on. The dispute is over whether that science tells the whole story.

differences.a: Something nonphysical, either a separate substance or irreducible mental properties of physical things.
differences.b: Brain activity, its functional roles, or other physical processes, with nothing nonphysical involved.

differences.a: The explanatory gap. Mary’s room and philosophical zombies suggest physical facts leave experience out.
differences.b: The tight dependence of experience on the brain, and the success of physical science everywhere else.

differences.a: The interaction problem. A nonphysical mind moving neurons seems to break the causal closure of physics.
differences.b: The hard problem. A full account of neural activity seems to leave open why it feels like anything.

differences.a: Hard to test directly, with no clear method for studying how a nonphysical mind works.
differences.b: Testable at the level of mechanisms through neuroscience, though the hard problem itself resists experiment.

differences.a: Substance dualism allows a soul to outlive the body, one reason most religions hold it.
differences.b: Consciousness ends when the brain stops working.

differences.a: Doubtful if minds are souls. Chalmers’s property dualism allows it for systems with the right functional organization.
differences.b: Possible on functionalist and computational views, doubted on biological ones.

orch-or-vs-iit.title: Orch OR vs Integrated Information Theory
orch-or-vs-iit.seoTitle: Orch OR vs IIT: Quantum Collapse vs Integrated Information
orch-or-vs-iit.metaDescription: Penrose and Hameroff tie consciousness to quantum events in microtubules. Tononi ties it to integrated information. Compare claims, tests and AI verdicts.
intro: Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch OR) and Integrated Information Theory (IIT) are among the few theories that place consciousness close to the foundations of physics, and both conclude that ordinary computers will never be conscious. They get there by very different routes.

Orch OR comes from the physicist Roger Penrose and the anesthesiologist Stuart Hameroff. In The Emperor’s New Mind, Penrose argued from Gödel’s incompleteness theorem that human understanding is not computable. He proposed that quantum superpositions collapse through an objective, gravity-related process, and Hameroff suggested where this happens in the brain, in microtubules inside neurons. Each orchestrated collapse is a moment of experience, and simpler proto-conscious events occur throughout the universe.

IIT, developed by Giulio Tononi and championed by Christof Koch, needs no new physics. It starts from features every experience has and identifies consciousness with integrated information, a system’s irreducible cause-effect structure, measured as Φ. Causal structure is what counts. Neuromorphic hardware wired like a brain could be conscious, while a brain simulation running on an ordinary computer would not be.

The two face different tests. Orch OR’s main challenge is decoherence. Max Tegmark calculated in 2000 that quantum states in the warm, wet brain should collapse far too fast to matter, and Hameroff and colleagues dispute his assumptions. IIT is criticized for predictions that defy common sense, such as consciousness in simple grids of logic gates, and for a measure too costly to compute on real brains.
orch-or-vs-iit.commonGround: Both deny that consciousness is computation, and both conclude that conventional digital computers running software will not be conscious. Both tie experience to physical structure at a deep level and give it a place in the basic description of nature. Critics have charged each with going beyond its evidence.

differences.a: Orchestrated collapse of quantum superpositions in neuronal microtubules, linked to the geometry of spacetime.
differences.b: Integrated information. An experience is identical to a system’s maximally irreducible cause-effect structure.

differences.a: New physics, a gravity-related collapse of the quantum state that current theory does not include.
differences.b: None beyond current physics. IIT applies to the causal structure of systems as they are now understood.

differences.a: Consciousness involves non-computable processes, so no algorithm, however complex, can produce it.
differences.b: Conventional chips have negligible Φ because of how their hardware is wired, whatever software they run.

differences.a: Decoherence. Critics doubt quantum coherence can last long enough in the warm, wet brain.
differences.b: Counterintuitive predictions, and a Φ measure that cannot be computed for real brains.

differences.a: Anesthetics and psychedelics acting on microtubules, and laboratory tests of gravity-related collapse.
differences.b: Studies of sleep, anesthesia and brain injury, and the Cogitate adversarial collaboration against Global Workspace Theory.

illusionism-vs-panpsychism.title: Illusionism vs Panpsychism
illusionism-vs-panpsychism.seoTitle: Illusionism vs Panpsychism: Is Experience What It Seems?
illusionism-vs-panpsychism.metaDescription: Illusionism says the felt qualities of experience are a trick of introspection. Panpsychism finds experience in all matter. Compare Frankish and Goff.
intro: Illusionism and panpsychism start from the same diagnosis and draw opposite conclusions. Both agree that standard physical science cannot explain phenomenal consciousness, the felt, qualitative character of experience, as it appears from the inside. Illusionists conclude that the appearance is mistaken. Panpsychists conclude that physics is incomplete.

Illusionism, defended by Keith Frankish and before him Daniel Dennett, holds that experience happens but qualia do not exist. Introspection gives us a simplified model of the brain’s own states, and that model misrepresents them as having ineffable inner qualities. Dennett compared this to a computer’s desktop, a user illusion that hides complex machinery. The job for science becomes what Frankish calls the illusion problem, explaining why brains are so convinced they have qualia.

Panpsychism, defended by Philip Goff, Galen Strawson and David Chalmers, takes those qualities at face value. Physics describes only what matter does, so its intrinsic nature may be experiential, and consciousness would then be present in the basic constituents of the world from the start.

Each side regards the other’s central claim as its weakness. Strawson has called the denial of consciousness the silliest claim ever made, since the existence of experience is the one thing we cannot be wrong about. Illusionists reply that introspection can mislead like any other sense, and that panpsychism keeps qualia at the cost of the combination problem and a claim no experiment can check. Goff and Frankish have argued the point at length, including on Mind Chat, the series they host together.
illusionism-vs-panpsychism.commonGround: Both agree that qualia as they appear cannot be reduced to brain processes, and both treat the hard problem as the central puzzle. They split on which side of it gives way. Both must also answer Chalmers’s meta-problem, why we judge that there is a hard problem at all.

differences.a: Qualia do not exist. Introspection represents brain states as having felt qualities they lack.
differences.b: Qualia are real and fundamental, present in simple form in the basic constituents of matter.

differences.a: Ordinary physical stuff as physics describes it, with nothing experiential added.
differences.b: Physical entities whose intrinsic nature is experiential or proto-experiential.

differences.a: An illusion of experience seems to be an experience itself, as John Searle and Galen Strawson argue.
differences.b: The combination problem. Nobody has shown how micro-experiences add up to a unified human mind.

differences.a: The illusion problem. Use neuroscience and psychology to explain why brains represent themselves as having qualia.
differences.b: Mainly philosophical. Solve the combination problem and show how experience fits within physics.

differences.a: Possible. A machine with the right functional organization would be conscious in the only sense illusionists accept.
differences.b: Open. AI hardware shares matter’s basic properties, and whether they combine into a subject is unresolved.
